headings: Who Are the Four Horsemen of Fear?
How the 4 Horsemen Disguise Themselves as Self-Sabotaging Behaviors
excerpts: The Four Horsemen of Fear - Corey Wilks, Psy.D. Skip to content Corey Wilks, Psy.D. Helping Creators Reach Their Potential Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Search Search Subscribe to the Newsletter Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Newsletter Search The Four Horsemen of Fear Lack of money, resources, or intelligence isn’t what holds entrepreneurs back from success. Limiting beliefs are. As a Clinical Psychologist and Executive Coach, I’ve noticed every limiting belief people struggle with falls into one of four categories. Everyone I’ve worked with—from bootstrapped first-time solopreneurs to VC-funded experienced founders—struggles with at least one of them. I call these limiting beliefs the Four Horsemen of Fear . In the last book of the Bible, Revelations , the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse spell doom for humanity. In business, and in life, the Four Horsemen of Fear spell doom for you, me, and anyone who wants to build something that matters. They wreak havoc on our psyches and keep us from realizing our potential by tricking us into unconsciously self-sabotaging. Who are these heralds of our mental destruction? Is there any hope to defeat them—to face our fear so we can do work that matters? Let’s dive in… ••• Who Are the Four Horsemen of Fear? The Horsemen are the four most common limiting beliefs that hold us back from putting ourselves out there and doing meaningful work. Some are easy to spot, some are sneaky, but all are conniving and whisper lies in our ears. The better you understand each, the easier you’ll spot them when they rear their heads. The 1st Horseman: Fear of Failure Everyone knows this one because it’s the easiest to identify. It sows doubts like: What if I’m not good enough? What if I can’t make this work? Fear of Failure keeps us from ever starting. But its lesser-known brethren are equally debilitating. The 2nd Horseman: Fear of Ridicule If you’ve ever let what critics think, or what “they” (your friends, family, society) might say, stop you from putting yourself out there or doing meaningful work—the 2nd Horseman has reared its ugly head. It whispers worries like: What if people judge me for doing this? What if they don’t like it? Fear of Ridicule tricks us into staying small and never taking a chance. The 3rd Horseman: Fear of Uncertainty The 3rd Horseman tells us we don’t have enough information to move forward. It whispers questions like: Which decision is right? Which direction should I choose? So we constantly seek more. More info. More resources. More answers. Fear of Uncertainty paralyzes us in a constant state of over-analysis. The 4th Horseman: Fear of Success This is the worst one because we deny its existence. Fear of Success holds more people back than Fear of Failure ever will. How could we be afraid of achieving the very thing we say we want? Because most of us believe success is a binary state: before and after. If we’ve never achieved success, we only know the “before” version of ourselves. “Post-success” us feels alien. Since we’re more familiar with our current state, we unconsciously self-sabotage to stay in familiar territory—to live in a world we understand. Achieving success represents crossing a threshold we can’t see beyond. And that’s terrifying. The 4th Horseman hides in thoughts like: If I succeed, will I lose my ambition? What if achieving success means I’ve peaked in life? What if I can’t balance power with responsibility? The Fourth Horseman tells us we’ll become a completely different person if we succeed, someone we won’t recognize. As this new person, we might become stagnant, corrupted by power, and ambitionless. Fear of Success tricks us into abandoning worthwhile projects right when we’re on the precipice of victory, to quit the race as soon as we get close enough to see the finish line. Every single limiting belief I’ve heard founders, creators, and entrepreneurs struggle with falls into one of the Horsemen’s domains. So how do you combat them? The first step is to recognize how the Horsemen disguise themselves in self-sabotaging behaviors: ••• How the 4 Horsemen Disguise Themselves as Self-Sabotaging Behaviors Self-sabotaging behaviors, no matter how destructive, serve a specific function —they help us avoid the thing we fear. Here are the most common self-sabotaging behaviors: Procrastination: The busier you stay, the more productive you are, right? Take on all the projects. Say yes to all the opportunities. Be a control freak and don’t outsource anything. Spend your time putting out every small fire that pops up. Spend hours getting to “inbox zero.” Have a hundred priorities, and never take responsibilities off your plate. Have a great new idea? Immediately chase it while leaving your current projects half-finished. Keep getting caught up in low ROI tasks instead of focusing on the Needle Movers . If you never finish, you never risk Failure or Success. Perfectionism and Imposter Syndrome: You don’t have all the answers. Your product isn’t ready yet. You don’t have enough authority for people to trust you. Who are you to build this? You’re a nobody. You’re unqualified. Better to wait until you learn more or create a better offer. Your competition is so far ahead of you, you’ll probably never catch up. So what’s the point of even trying? You should wait until you feel ready, then you won’t have anything to be afraid of. How long have you been “writing” your book or article, but still won’t publish it? How long have you been thinking about, or actually building, that project but still haven’t shipped it? How long have you thought out every possible scenario and created the “perfect” plan, but still haven’t taken the steps to go from idea to execution? As long as you don’t put yourself out there, you avoid Ridicule. Complacency: Too many entrepreneurs create golden handcuffs (soul-sucking. but lucrative, businesses) and willingly choose to stay shackled than face the uncertainty freedom could bring. Most people would rather choose the path that leads to predictable misery than the one that offers the chance of a better life. Humans are creatures of habit. We gravitate toward what we can anticipate. Uncertainty is terrifying. Staying in your comfort zone keeps you safe from Uncertainty. Now you know each of the Four Horsemen of Fear, how they disguise themselves, and why we self-sabotage. But how can you overcome them? pages.title: Liminal Tension: A New Way to Think About Imposter Syndrome - Corey Wilks, Psy.D.
pages.description: What if Imposter Syndrome wasn't a sign to back off, but actually a good sign? Here's why seeing Imposter Syndrome as "Liminal Tension" can help...
headings: Liminal Tension: A New Way to Think About Imposter Syndrome
Traversing Liminality: The Function of Rites of Passage
How to Become Your Ideal Future Self Today
The Parvum Opus Method to Overcoming Writer’s Block
excerpts: Liminal Tension: A New Way to Think About Imposter Syndrome - Corey Wilks, Psy.D. Skip to content Corey Wilks, Psy.D. Helping Creators Reach Their Potential Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Search Search Subscribe to the Newsletter Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Resources Articles Podcast YouTube Services 1:1 Coaching Workshops & Keynotes Audit + Strategy Session Inner Game Intensive Newsletter Search Liminal Tension: A New Way to Think About Imposter Syndrome Quick Note: If you’d rather check out the audio/video version of this article, you can get it on YouTube , Spotify , Apple , or Other Places you get your podcasts. No matter how much expertise, ambition, or discipline you have—Imposter Syndrome will always hold you back from fully stepping into what you know you’re capable of. A lot of the work I do as a psychologist-turned-executive coach is helping founders, leaders, and creators remove the psychological bottlenecks costing them business growth, and Imposter Syndrome is one of the most common psychological bottlenecks I see. Imposter Syndrome is often a symptom of Fear of Ridicule (one of the Four Horsemen of Fear ), and it holds many of us back from putting ourselves and our ideas out into the world. Because Imposter Syndrome, fundamentally, is the belief that you don’t belong in the room—whatever that room is (physical, virtual, or conceptual). So if you attempt to enter that room, you feel a cognitive resistance—a tension—that most people interpret as a sign to back off. But what if it wasn’t a sign to back off? I personally hate the term “Imposter Syndrome,” because it completely misdiagnoses what you’re going through. Instead, I like to use the term “Liminal Tension,” and here’s why… The Problem with Imposter Syndrome When you mentally label the tension you feel as “Imposter Syndrome,” it makes you think you’re a fraud who doesn’t belong. So anytime you start to enter a room and feel that tension, you pull back and tell yourself you need to wait until you feel “ready” or “prepared” before you try to enter the room again. “Then,” you tell yourself, “I’ll belong in the room.” Because everyone else in that room clearly deserves to be there because they have more expertise, more success, or are somehow superior to you in some way. This is why labeling it as Imposter Syndrome holds you back. You have integrity, so you obviously don’t want people to think you’re a fraud, and you definitely don’t want to feel like a fraud internally. So you wait until that magical day where you won’t feel like a fraud before you enter those bigger, better, scarier rooms. But that day never comes, so you spend your entire life pulling back every time you’re on the precipice of a new room. And again, that “new room” can be a physical one like speaking at a conference, a conceptual one like publishing a book that could sit on the same shelf as your favorite authors, or even an identity one like shifting from seeing yourself as a solopreneur of a tiny company to a CEO of a company you’re scaled into a “real” business. Instead, you can learn to see that exact same tension as a good sign—a sign to lean in instead of pull back. If you re-label it as Liminal Tension. But what does that mean? A liminal space is the area between two things. It’s like a hallway between two rooms. While you’re in the hallway, you’re on your way from one room to the other, but you’re not in either. And right as you’re about to enter the room the hallway leads to, you have to cross the threshold to that new room. It’s at this threshold that we feel maximum tension because it’s the final step before we actually enter the new room—the room we’ve maybe never been in before. And since we’ve never been in this room before, it’s easy to doubt ourselves into believing we don’t belong in the room. I’ve experienced this in my own life. Identity Ambiguity I wrote online for about a year before I allowed myself to identify as a writer. Because I kept comparing myself to “real” writers who’d been doing it for years or bestselling authors. Of course I didn’t belong in the room with these writers—I was just starting out and finding my voice. Then one day one of my favorite writers reached out and said they loved my writing—now we’re friends. Then another writer who’d inspired me brought me on to collaborate on a writing project. Then writers started sending me their books, thanking me in their bestselling books ( check out my episode with Ali Abdaal ), asking to come on my podcast to talk about the craft of writing ( check out my episode with Lawrence Yeo ). Then I got invited to exclusive writer meetups with bestselling authors and deca-millionaires with writing businesses. But was I real writer? Am I real writer now? Do I belong in the room of real writers? When do I belong in the room of real writers? The same tension holds anytime we try to cross the threshold to enter a new room. When you try to take action that doesn’t align with your identity, you experience cognitive dissonance—which feels like mental static or anxiety because there’s a discrepancy between your self-belief and behavior. Which means if you want to take action to enter the room, you have to believe you belong in the room in the first place. Otherwise, you’ll self-sabotage (aka, change your behavior) to preserve the belief that you don’t belong in the room. Put another way, identity is the foundation of aligned action. If you don’t believe you’re worthy of being in the room, you won’t take action to enter the room. I see this all the time in my work with founders. Highly ambitious, accomplished, and disciplined people memorizing all the productivity “hacks” and trying to take action over and over but always somehow sabotaging their success at the last minute. Because their identity is holding them back (which is one reason so many people have a fear of success ). It’s not woo-woo to say you have to believe in yourself. It’s human psychology. Our behaviors are downstream of our beliefs. Everything we do, every action we take and every thought we have, is rooted in our beliefs (about ourselves and the world around us). We’re driven to reinforce our own schema of the world and ourselves, meaning we take actions that align with what we believe is true, possible, and deserved. So if you believe you belong in the room, you’ll take the action of crossing the threshold. If you believe you don’t belong in the room, you’ll take the action to avoid crossing the threshold. But if you learn to label that feeling as Liminal Tension, a sign you’re challenging yourself to grow, it’s much easier to cross that threshold. Because you’re not expecting perfection, you’re pursuing progress. When I decided to become a public speaker and lead workshops and presentations for entrepreneurship conferences, there was obviously a point where I’d never done it before and had to cross the threshold into leading my first one. I could’ve easily told myself I didn’t belong in the room—or “Who am I to call myself a public speaker?”—but instead I reframed it as “Stepping into this opportunity, this room, will help me grow into the person I know I’m capable of.” I had to lean into the liminal tension that came up as I crossed the threshold from being not-a-speaker to being a speaker. That liminal tension will always be there when you attempt to enter a new room because it represents the threshold of a new identity, a new skillset, a new life. What you’re feeling is the tension of growth, of evolution, of actualizing your potential. Seeing it as liminal tension helps you reframe the initial belief of “This is a room I don’t belong in” into “This is a room where I’ll grow in.” And that allows you to take the aligned action of leaning in instead of pulling back to stay in your comfort zone. But the reason we struggle so much to navigate this liminal tension comes down to human psychology. Traversing Liminality: The Function of Rites of Passage We don’t have rites of passage anymore, at least not at a societal level. Think about it—when did you know you were an adult? What makes you an adult? Is it when you turn 18? Get a job? Graduate? Have kids? Get a mortgage? Sneeze and almost bust a rib? Groan when he get up from the couch? So here you are, in your mid-30s and still look around the room for a “real adult,” only to realize that’s you. A rite of passage offers a clear path to traverse the liminal space between two states. Without these, it’s hard to know when we’ve officially crossed the chasm and “arrived.” Rites of passage are an antidote to Imposter Syndrome because they codify what it means to belong in the room. They offer clear structure and support to navigate the journey along with a concrete definition of when you’re “arrived.” If you survive this trial, you belong. If you don’t survive this trial, keep trying until you do—then you’ll belong. It might still feel surreal to be in the room, but you’ll know you belong because you passed the test. There are clear parameters. But we don’t have these anymore, so we don’t have guidance on how to traverse the liminal. All we have is the tension we feel when we try to cross the threshold of the door leading to the room we deeply want to be in, which causes us to doubt we belong. Now, you could try to come up with some elaborate ritual to act as a rite of passage to help you navigate this liminal tension. Or you can learn to see this Liminal Tension itself as a rite of passage into a new identity, a new reality, a new life. Because everyone who’s ever inspired you constantly sought liminal tension and expanded their growth edges, which is why they continually leveled up and became a better and better version of themselves. Final Thoughts “The fastest way to change your life is to force yourself to level up by placing yourself in an environment where you feel like you don’t belong.” — Jay Yang Take a second and reflect. There’s a room right now that you’ve been at the threshold of entering for a while now, but keep pulling back because you label that discomfort as Imposter Syndrome. But “Imposter Syndrome” is a terrible misdiagnosis of what you’re experiencing. You’re not a fraud. You’re evolving. But the longer you delay entering that room, the longer you delay your own evolution. And you have too much potential to keep doing that. What if instead, you chose to see that tension as a sign of growth and decided to lean into it? What if you told yourself, “This tension is supposed to be here. I’m supposed to feel this because it means I’m growing and pushing myself.” How would that change how you act right now? Pull out a notecard and write down this reminder: The growth you seek is in the room you’re avoiding. Liminal Tension is a much better term. So what tension will you lean into? What evolution will you finally give yourself permission to embrace? What new identity will you step into? Let me know—I’d love to learn more about you. Read Next: The Four Horsemen of Fear P.S. You know your business is capable of more—that you are capable of more—yet you feel stuck despite all your ambitious, discipline, and achievements so far. raw.title: Corey Wilks: Extracted Judgment Model
raw.creator_judgment_model: The creator appears to judge entrepreneurial and creative progress primarily through an inner-game lens: visible performance problems are often interpreted as expressions of underlying fear, limiting beliefs, identity conflict, or avoidance. The preferred response is to identify the psychological pattern, reinterpret the discomfort or behavior, and take aligned action toward meaningful work and a more expansive identity. This is a calibration hypothesis based on the bounded pages, not a definitive account of the creator's full model.

frameworks.name: Four Horsemen of Fear
frameworks.creator_distinction: The creator distinguishes four recurring categories of limiting belief: fear of failure, fear of ridicule, fear of uncertainty, and fear of success.
observable_evidence: The page states that limiting beliefs fall into four categories.
Fear of failure is associated with not starting.
Fear of ridicule is associated with concern about judgment and staying small.
Fear of uncertainty is associated with over-analysis and seeking more information.
Fear of success is associated with self-sabotage near achievement and preserving a familiar identity.
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/ — “I call these limiting beliefs the Four Horsemen of Fear.”
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/ — headings and descriptions for “Fear of Failure,” “Fear of Ridicule,” “Fear of Uncertainty,” and “Fear of Success.”
calibration_questions: Does the creator intend these four categories to be exhaustive, or are they a practical heuristic?
How does the creator distinguish among overlapping fears in a specific case?
What evidence would cause the creator to reject a fear-based interpretation?

frameworks.name: Self-sabotage as fear avoidance
frameworks.creator_distinction: The creator distinguishes the surface behavior from the feared outcome it may help a person avoid; procrastination, perfectionism, imposter feelings, and complacency are presented as potentially functional avoidance strategies rather than simple discipline failures.
observable_evidence: The page says self-sabotaging behaviors “serve a specific function” by helping people avoid what they fear.
Procrastination is linked to unfinished work and avoidance of failure or success.
Perfectionism and imposter feelings are linked to avoiding ridicule by delaying publication or action.
Complacency is linked to avoiding uncertainty by remaining in predictable conditions.
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/ — “Self-sabotaging behaviors, no matter how destructive, serve a specific function—they help us avoid the thing we fear.”
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/ — sections “Procrastination,” “Perfectionism and Imposter Syndrome,” and “Complacency.”
calibration_questions: Does the creator treat the inferred avoided fear as a hypothesis to test or as the usual explanation?
What alternative explanations does the creator consider for the same behavior?
How should a respondent distinguish protective delay from fear-driven avoidance?

frameworks.name: Liminal Tension
frameworks.creator_distinction: The creator distinguishes between interpreting discomfort at the edge of a new role as evidence of fraud or non-belonging and interpreting the same discomfort as tension associated with identity transition and growth.
observable_evidence: The creator proposes replacing “Imposter Syndrome” with “Liminal Tension.”
Tension is described as occurring near the threshold of a new room, identity, skillset, or life.
The recommended reinterpretation is to see the tension as a sign to lean in rather than pull back.
The creator contrasts waiting to feel ready with pursuing progress while entering a new identity.

What observable criteria indicate that a person is ready to cross a threshold?

frameworks.name: Identity as a condition of aligned action
frameworks.creator_distinction: The creator distinguishes actions that fit a person's current self-belief from actions that require adopting or practicing a broader identity; perceived non-belonging is presented as capable of producing behavioral retreat.

missing_evidence: No bounded page establishes how the creator prioritizes psychological explanations against structural, financial, interpersonal, health, or situational explanations.

raw.claim_boundary: This extraction reports distinctions explicitly presented or strongly indicated in the supplied public-page captures. Interpretations about the creator's broader judgment model remain calibration hypotheses. The evidence does not justify diagnosing respondents, treating the Four Horsemen or Liminal Tension as validated measures, inferring stable traits, or assuming that discomfort, delay, or underperformance is caused by fear or identity conflict.

raw.title: Creator Judgment Model: Corey Wilks, Psy.D. (bounded public capture, 2026-10-12)
raw.creator_judgment_model: Observed in the captured pages: the creator treats business and creative stalls as primarily psychological rather than skill, resource, or information deficits. The homepage states the work is 'the inner game' and 'the deeply psychological, existential, and identity-level aspects still capping your potential.' The Four Horsemen page states that 'Lack of money, resources, or intelligence isn't what holds entrepreneurs back from success. Limiting beliefs are.' The creator's working distinctions appear to be: (1) limiting beliefs as the primary bottleneck; (2) identity as the foundation of action, stated as 'identity is the foundation of aligned action' and 'Our behaviors are downstream of our beliefs'; (3) self-sabotage as functional avoidance, stated as self-sabotaging behaviors 'serve a specific function—they help us avoid the thing we fear'; (4) discomfort at a threshold is reinterpreted as growth ('Liminal Tension') rather than as evidence of unreadiness or fraud. The model is presented as the creator's own clinical-coaching synthesis; the captured pages do not show validation data, outcome measures, or how the categories were derived. Interpretation: the creator's judgment appears to rank internal belief structures above external constraints when diagnosing stalled progress, and to treat 'readiness' as a belief-mediated state rather than a condition to be met first.

frameworks.name: The Four Horsemen of Fear
frameworks.creator_distinction: Creator distinguishes four categories of limiting belief (Failure, Ridicule, Uncertainty, Success) and asserts that every limiting belief the creator has encountered falls into one of them. The distinction between 'Fear of Success' and 'Fear of Failure' as separate categories, with Fear of Success described as the most denied, is a stated creator distinction.
observable_evidence: 'As a Clinical Psychologist and Executive Coach, I've noticed every limiting belief people struggle with falls into one of four categories.'
'Every single limiting belief I've heard founders, creators, and entrepreneurs struggle with falls into one of the Horsemen's domains.'
'This is the worst one because we deny its existence. Fear of Success holds more people back than Fear of Failure ever will.'
Each horseman is given a sample self-talk line (e.g., 'What if I'm not good enough?'; 'What if people judge me for doing this?'; 'Which decision is right?'; 'If I succeed, will I lose my ambition?').

raw.claim_boundary: This analysis describes the creator's stated judgment distinctions as they appear in a bounded capture of four public pages (homepage, Four Horsemen, Articles index, Liminal Tension). It does not establish the creator's actual clinical practice, the validity or reliability of the categories, causal relations between beliefs and behavior, or outcomes for clients or readers. Confidence ratings reflect how explicitly and repeatedly a distinction appears in the captured text, not its empirical support. Interpretive phrasings (e.g., 'appears to rank internal belief structures above external constraints') are calibration hypotheses for building respondent instruments, not findings about the creator's traits or motives. Pages were truncated to 12,000 characters, so unseen material may qualify or contradict these distinctions.

raw.title: Respondent Instrument: Attribution and Judgment of Stalled Progress (derived from Corey Wilks, Psy.D. bounded public capture, 2026-10-12)

dimensions.name: Primary attribution of a stalled goal
dimensions.note: Categorical classification of which explanation the respondent first treats as the bottleneck (internal belief, skill, resource/time, external context). No category is scored as healthier or better. The creator's model prioritizes belief-level explanations; this dimension records the respondent's own ordering and whether it is tested against alternatives.
observable_manifestations: Names a single first-line explanation for a stall
Lists alternative explanations and the evidence used to rank them
Changes the ranking after a disconfirming observation
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/

dimensions.name: Avoidance-function reading of self-sabotaging behavior
dimensions.note: Records whether the respondent interprets a recurring avoidance behavior as serving to avoid a specific feared outcome, and whether they can name the alternative explanation (skill gap, workload, external constraint) that would account for the same behavior.
observable_manifestations: Links a specific avoided task to a named feared outcome
Names a non-avoidance explanation for the same task pattern
States what observation would distinguish avoidance from the alternative
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/

dimensions.name: Interpretation of threshold tension
dimensions.note: Categorical reading of the discomfort felt before entering an unfamiliar role, room, or output type: unreadiness signal, fraud signal, developmental-transition signal, or no distinct signal. Captures how the respondent labels tension and what they do next, without treating the creator's relabeling as correct.
observable_manifestations: Chooses a labeling of threshold tension
Describes the action taken after the label
Specifies conditions under which tension should prompt stopping
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/

dimensions.name: Sequencing of identity, belief, and action
dimensions.note: Categorical classification of whether the respondent expects identity or belief to change before action, action before belief change, or a bidirectional or condition-dependent sequence. The creator's stated sequence is identity-first; the instrument tests whether respondents can specify observations that would change their sequencing view.
observable_manifestations: Selects an action-first or identity-first sequence for a described case
Proposes a small test whose result would update belief
States a disconfirming outcome for their chosen sequence
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/

dimensions.name: Category assignment rule for limiting beliefs
dimensions.note: Categorical record of how the respondent assigns their own limiting beliefs to categories (fear of failure, ridicule, uncertainty, success, or none), including whether they have a decision rule for beliefs that fit more than one category. Tests the partition rather than assuming it is exhaustive.
observable_manifestations: Assigns verbatim self-statements to categories with a stated rule
Flags statements that do not fit any category
Flags statements that fit two or more categories and states how they were handled
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/

dimensions.name: External threshold markers
dimensions.note: Categorical record of whether the respondent relies on external or self-defined markers to decide they have crossed a threshold (credentials, outside recognition, a self-set completion criterion, none). Low confidence because the creator's cultural-historical claim about rites of passage is not supported in the captured pages.
observable_manifestations: Names the marker used to decide arrival
States whether the marker is external or self-defined
Describes a case where the marker was met but the threshold still felt unresolved
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/

questions.text: A project you care about has not shipped in six weeks. Rank these explanations from most to least likely for your own case, then state the single piece of evidence that moved your top choice: (a) a skill you have not yet built, (b) limited time or money, (c) a belief about your readiness or identity, (d) an external factor such as market timing or platform changes.
questions.behavior_being_tested: How the respondent ranks and justifies attribution of a stall across internal and external explanations.
questions.input_spec: Rank four listed explanations and provide one sentence of evidence for the top-ranked item.
response_options: a: skill gap
b: time or money constraint
c: belief or identity
d: external factor
Other (specify)
questions.scoring_logic: Record the top-ranked category and whether the evidence sentence references an observation (categorical). Do not score belief-first rankings as more or less accurate.
questions.strong_signal: Top choice is supported by a specific observation, and the respondent names what would change the ranking.
questions.weak_signal: Top choice is given with no evidence, or evidence is a restatement of the choice.
confounders: Recent failure or public criticism shifting attribution
Financial pressure unrelated to the stalled goal
Respondent expectation that a coaching-oriented instrument favors internal explanations
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/

questions.name: Log two weeks of avoided tasks. For each entry, record the task, the outcome you feared, and one non-avoidance explanation (skill, workload, outside constraint) that would account for the same skipping. Then state one observation that would distinguish the avoidance explanation from the non-avoidance explanation.
questions.behavior_being_tested: Whether the respondent can generate and test alternative explanations for repeated task avoidance instead of accepting a single function-based account.
questions.input_spec: Dated log of at least five avoided tasks, each with columns: task; feared outcome (or none); alternative explanation; distinguishing observation. Submit as a table or list.
questions.scoring_logic: Categorical: (i) avoidance explanation linked to a named feared outcome, (ii) at least one alternative explanation per entry, (iii) a distinguishing observation that could be collected. Count entries meeting all three.
questions.strong_signal: Entries include alternative explanations and distinguishing observations, and at least one entry where the alternative is judged more likely.
questions.weak_signal: All entries name the same feared outcome with no alternatives, or feared outcomes are unspecified.
confounders: Selective recall of avoided tasks
Log written after the fact rather than contemporaneously
Respondent treating the log as a test of their character
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/

questions.name: You are about to enter a room you have not entered before (a conference stage, a first client category, a new role). You notice tension. Which label best matches what you would actually do next?
questions.behavior_being_tested: Interpretation of threshold tension and the action that follows it.
questions.input_spec: Select one label and describe in one sentence the action you would take in the next 24 hours.
response_options: Unreadiness: pause until more preparation is done
Fraud signal: I may not belong and should reconsider
Developmental transition: proceed with the entry and observe
No distinct signal: the tension does not change my decision
Depends on specified conditions (describe)
questions.scoring_logic: Categorical label plus the stated next action. Record whether label and action are consistent. No label is scored as correct.
questions.strong_signal: Label is paired with a specific action and a condition under which the respondent would reverse the choice.
questions.weak_signal: Label is chosen without an action, or action contradicts the label without comment.
confounders: Recent exposure to the 'Imposter Syndrome' or 'Liminal Tension' terms
Stakes of the room (financial, reputational) changing the response
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/

questions.name: Case: A creator has written for a year but has not yet described themselves as a writer, and has been offered a speaking slot they feel unready for. Choose the sequence you think is more likely to produce the next change, then name one observation that would show you were wrong.
questions.behavior_being_tested: Whether the respondent prioritizes identity-first or action-first sequencing and can name a disconfirming observation.
questions.input_spec: Choose one option and write one sentence naming the disconfirming observation.
response_options: Identity first: the creator must believe they are a writer before taking the speaking slot
Action first: taking the slot and observing the result is more likely to update the belief
Condition-dependent: the sequence depends on a stated factor (name it)
Neither is clearly more likely
questions.scoring_logic: Categorical choice of sequence plus presence or absence of a disconfirming observation.
questions.strong_signal: Choice is accompanied by a specific, observable disconfirming result.
questions.weak_signal: Choice is given with no disconfirming observation, or the observation cannot be observed.
confounders: Respondent's familiarity with identity-based coaching language
Preference for a particular domain (writing versus speaking) unrelated to sequencing
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/

questions.name: Take three self-statements you have recently used to explain why you have not started or finished something. Assign each to one of four categories: fear of failure, fear of ridicule, fear of uncertainty, fear of success, or none. State the rule you used. Mark any statement that fits two categories and say how you decided.
questions.behavior_being_tested: Whether the respondent can apply a stated category rule to their own statements and handle multi-category or no-category cases.
questions.input_spec: Three verbatim self-statements, each with a category assignment, a one-sentence rule, and a note on ambiguity if applicable.
questions.scoring_logic: Categorical: (i) rule stated, (ii) at least one ambiguous or unassignable case recorded, (iii) ambiguous cases resolved with an explicit rule rather than forced assignment.
questions.strong_signal: Rule is stated, and at least one statement is recorded as not fitting or as fitting two categories with a stated resolution.
questions.weak_signal: All three statements are assigned without a rule, and none are recorded as ambiguous.
confounders: Respondent choosing statements that fit the categories well
Familiarity with the four-category framework prompting forced fit
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/the-four-horsemen-of-fear/

questions.name: Name one observation that would lead you to stop pursuing a goal even though you feel threshold tension about it. Then name one observation that would lead you to continue despite a skill or resource gap you can identify.
questions.behavior_being_tested: Whether the respondent specifies conditions under which tension should not be read as a reason to proceed, and conditions under which a skill or resource gap should dominate.
questions.input_spec: Two observations, each one sentence, labeled 'stop' and 'continue despite gap'.
questions.scoring_logic: Categorical: stop-condition present (yes/no), continue-despite-gap condition present (yes/no), and whether both are observable.
questions.strong_signal: Both conditions are stated and are observable without relying on feelings alone.
questions.weak_signal: Only feeling-based conditions are named, or neither condition is named.
confounders: Strong attachment to the goal reducing willingness to name stop conditions
Ambiguity in what counts as a skill gap
source_basis: https://coreywilkspsyd.com/liminal-tension-imposter-syndrome/
https://coreywilkspsyd.com/

raw.claim_boundary: Score semantics are categorical: each dimension and question classifies attribution, labeling, sequencing, or rule-use patterns. No category is treated as healthy, accurate, or better, and high or low values are not defined. This instrument is derived from stated distinctions in four bounded public pages (homepage, Four Horsemen, Articles index, Liminal Tension) and does not establish the creator's clinical practice, the validity or reliability of the categories, causal relations between belief and behavior, or outcomes for any audience. Interpretive phrasings in the source model are calibration hypotheses, not findings about the creator or respondents. Items are designed to elicit behavior, decisions, scenarios, and inspectable artifacts, not agreement with the creator's worldview. Pages were truncated at 12,000 characters, so unseen material may qualify these distinctions.
missing_evidence: Full bodies of Fear Inoculation, Action Gap, How to Make Success Inevitable, The Hidden Cost of Success, and Metacognition articles (titles and teasers only).
Derivation method for the four Horsemen categories and any validation or reliability data.
Operational definitions of identity, belief, self-actualization, and readiness.
Explicit criteria for psychological versus skill, resource, or context bottlenecks.
Stated conditions under which the model does not apply or a horseman assignment fails.
Podcast, video, or workshop transcripts in which the creator explains the framework at length.
Scope and provenance of the cultural-historical claim about rites of passage.
Collection and selection method for testimonials.
Credential claims (Psy.D., Clinical Psychologist) were not evaluated.
